config.editorData:
Backpressure — is vSAN throttling itself, and which layer is doing it?

Congestion is vSAN telling you it has deliberately slowed something down to protect itself. It is not an error and it is not a failure — it is a control signal, and the useful question is never is there congestion but which layer raised it and why.

Read this screen top down. The cluster tables say whether the whole cluster is under pressure. The per-host tables say whether it is one host. The RDT tables at the bottom say whether the problem is the network transport rather than the storage at all — which is the single most commonly misdiagnosed case, because every layer above reports congestion when the transport underneath is starved.

The congestion TYPE is the diagnosis. Read congestion and write congestion point at different causes and different fixes. Unmap congestion is space reclamation competing with guest IO. Resync read congestion means rebuild traffic is the source, which is usually correct behaviour and self-clearing — the cluster is choosing redundancy over latency, and it will stop when the rebuild does.

Component congestion against shared congestion is the host-versus-device call. Component congestion isolated to one object points at a device; shared congestion across a host points at the host. Acting on the wrong one replaces healthy hardware.

On the RDT tables, kaReset deserves attention out of proportion to its size. Keepalive resets mean the transport dropped and re-established, and they survive a NIC that looks perfectly healthy on every error counter. Small buffer minima (txSbSpaceMin, rxSbSpaceMin) next to a rising queue latency is the signature of a transport running out of room rather than a disk running slow.

Cluster - front end congestion

Renders the vSAN Cluster DOM Client view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Broadcom's own threshold for this metric is 15 ms warning and 30 ms critical, published in the Performance Service graph definition as yellow=15000 red=30000 microseconds, direction upper. That is a badly-wrong line rather than a tuning line -- a healthy cluster here runs under 1.5 ms, so the product only flags at roughly ten times normal. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it. Product threshold 15 ms warning, 30 ms critical.

Congestions — vSAN's own backpressure signal, raised when a layer cannot absorb the offered load and asks the layer above to slow down. Zero on a healthy cluster, and it reads zero here. Any sustained non-zero value is the single most important number on the screen.

Read Congestions — Backpressure attributed to reads.

Write Congestions — Backpressure attributed to writes.

Unmap congestion — Backpressure attributed to unmap and space-reclamation work.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read at this layer.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written at this layer.

Cluster - owner congestion

Renders the vSAN Cluster DOM Owner view.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Broadcom's own threshold for this metric is 15 ms warning and 30 ms critical, published in the Performance Service graph definition as yellow=15000 red=30000 microseconds, direction upper. That is a badly-wrong line rather than a tuning line -- a healthy cluster here runs under 1.5 ms, so the product only flags at roughly ten times normal. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it. Product threshold 15 ms warning, 30 ms critical.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read. The owner layer names its throughput columns differently from the client layer; the quantity is the same.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Congestions — vSAN's own backpressure signal, raised when a layer cannot absorb the offered load and asks the layer above to slow down. Zero on a healthy cluster, and it reads zero here. Any sustained non-zero value is the single most important number on the screen.

Read Congestions — Backpressure attributed to reads.

Write Congestions — Backpressure attributed to writes.

Back end - device vs host

Renders the vSAN Host DOM Component Manager view.

Component congestion — Congestion raised against a single component -- one object's share of one device. Isolated to one component on one host it points at that DEVICE. Compare it with shared congestion on the same row: component high and shared low means the device, both high means the host.

Shared congestion — Congestion on capacity shared across the host rather than attributable to one component. High here with component congestion low means the HOST is the constraint, not any individual disk. Replacing a device on this reading changes nothing.

Resync read congestion — Congestion caused specifically by rebuild reads. Usually correct behaviour rather than a fault: the cluster is choosing to restore redundancy and accepting latency to do it. Self-clearing when the rebuild finishes. Act on it only if the rebuild itself is not progressing -- check the Resync screen before touching anything here.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Broadcom's own threshold for this metric is 15 ms warning and 30 ms critical, published in the Performance Service graph definition as yellow=15000 red=30000 microseconds, direction upper. That is a badly-wrong line rather than a tuning line -- a healthy cluster here runs under 1.5 ms, so the product only flags at roughly ten times normal. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Latency (max, read) — Worst read latency in the interval. Read beside the average: a large gap is a tail-latency problem, which guests feel as stalls even when the average looks fine.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it. Product threshold 15 ms warning, 30 ms critical.

Latency (max, write) — Worst write latency in the interval. Measured here at 14.9 ms against a 957 microsecond average -- a fifteenfold tail on an idle cluster, and the kind of thing an average hides completely.

Latency standard deviation (write) — Spread of write latency. High spread with a low average means the work is bimodal: most operations fast, some very slow.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Read Throughput — Bytes per second read at this layer.

Write Throughput — Bytes per second written at this layer.

VM disk queue depth (write) — Queue depth for writes to virtual disk objects at the component manager. Depth is the cause; the latency columns are the effect.

VM disk dispatched cost (write) — Accumulated cost of dispatched virtual disk writes, in vSAN's internal scheduling units. Not comparable to a time or a byte count -- useful for comparing hosts against each other, not against a threshold.

Namespace dispatched cost (write) — The same cost measure for namespace objects, which hold VM configuration rather than guest data. Large values here with small virtual disk values mean the work is metadata, not guest IO.

Owner - reclaim and rebuild

Renders the vSAN Host DOM Owner view.

Seg cleaner unmap congestion — Congestion from the segment cleaner reclaiming space. On ESA this competes with guest IO and with rebuild traffic for the same devices, so it rises when the cluster is both busy and reclaiming. Sustained high values with free capacity falling is the combination worth acting on; briefly high on its own is routine housekeeping.

Resync Read Congestions — Congestion from recovery writes -- the write half of restoring redundancy. Its official name from the Performance Service is "Resync Read Congestions", which contradicts its id. The label is Broadcom's and is reproduced rather than corrected; treat the id as authoritative and see BACKLOG.md.

Write Latency — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it. Product threshold 15 ms warning, 30 ms critical.

Latency (max, write) — Worst write latency in the interval. Measured here at 14.9 ms against a 957 microsecond average -- a fifteenfold tail on an idle cluster, and the kind of thing an average hides completely.

Latency standard deviation (write) — Spread of write latency. High spread with a low average means the work is bimodal: most operations fast, some very slow.

Read Latency — Average read latency at this layer. Broadcom's own threshold for this metric is 15 ms warning and 30 ms critical, published in the Performance Service graph definition as yellow=15000 red=30000 microseconds, direction upper. That is a badly-wrong line rather than a tuning line -- a healthy cluster here runs under 1.5 ms, so the product only flags at roughly ten times normal. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Latency (max, read) — Worst read latency in the interval. Read beside the average: a large gap is a tail-latency problem, which guests feel as stalls even when the average looks fine.

High outstanding IO duration percent (write) — Proportion of the interval the owner spent with its write queue above its high-watermark. Measured at 3% here on an otherwise idle cluster. This is the metric vCenter surfaces as a top-line vSAN indicator, and it moves well before average latency does.

Owner2 pc commit latency avg us — Time to commit a write across its replicas using two-phase commit. This is the irreducible cost of making a write durable in more than one place, and it sets the floor under every write latency above it.

Write leaf owner latency local — Write latency for replicas that live on this host, so no network is involved.

Write leaf owner latency remote — Write latency for replicas on other hosts, which includes the network round trip. Read as a pair with the local column: remote should be the slower of the two, and when it is not, the local disks are the problem.

Read leaf owner latency local — Read latency served from this host's own disks. Measured at 1392 microseconds here against 905 for remote reads -- local slower than across the network, which inverts the expected order and points at a local device rather than the fabric.

Read leaf owner latency remote — Read latency served from another host's disks, network included.

Server switch count — Lifetime count of ownership changes: how often coordination of an object moved from one host to another. Cumulative since boot, so the value means little; a rate that climbs means objects are being handed around, which costs latency.

IOPS — Total operations per second at this layer, reads and writes together.

Outstanding IO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Is vSAN throttling itself?

Renders the vSAN Host DOM Owner Scheduler view.

Num net sched rolling avg latency us — The rolling average latency vSAN's own scheduler is working from. This is the input to its throttling decisions, not an observation of guest latency.

Num net sched guest lt latency us — Guest long-tail latency as the scheduler measures it. What it is trying to protect.

Num net sched low band thresh us — The latency threshold at which the scheduler moves a host into its low band. Context for the band counters -- without it they are unreadable.

Num net sched low band — Times the scheduler placed this host in its low band, meaning it decided latency was bad enough to throttle rebuild and resync traffic hard to protect guest IO.

Num net sched mid band — Times the scheduler placed this host in its middle band: some throttling, latency elevated but not severe.

Num net sched low band sec — Seconds spent in the low band. More useful than the count beside it -- one long episode and many brief ones are different problems.

Num net sched mid band sec — Seconds spent in the middle band.

Num net sched low to mid band — Transitions from the low band up to the middle band, meaning conditions improved.

Num net sched mid to low band — Transitions from the middle band down to the low band, meaning conditions worsened. A host oscillating between bands is unstable in a way neither band counter alone reveals.

Num net sched seen total tp bps — Total throughput the scheduler observed, guest and rebuild traffic together.

Num net sched seen non resync tp bps — Throughput excluding resync. Subtract it from the total to see what rebuild traffic is actually consuming -- the pair answers 'is the rebuild hurting the guests'.

Num net sched controller IOPS limit — The IOPS ceiling the scheduler is currently imposing. A limit far above actual load means it is not intervening.

Transport - cluster

Renders the vSAN Cluster RDT view.

RDT Network Max Outbound Context Bytes — The high-water mark of bytes queued for transmit on an RDT context. A rising maximum alongside a healthy average means the transport is bursting into its headroom rather than sitting in it -- the early signal, before queue latency moves. Read it next to txSbSpaceMin: a high maximum with a low buffer minimum is a transport running out of room, and no amount of disk tuning will help.

RDT Network Cluster Average Latency — Average round-trip latency of vSAN's own transport between hosts. This sits above TCP, so it can be slow while every NIC counter is clean.

RDT Network Cluster Max Latency — Worst round-trip latency observed. Spikes here matter more than the average -- one stalled transfer blocks whatever was waiting on it.

RDT Network Cluster Min Latency — Best round-trip latency observed. Useful only as a floor to compare the average against.

RDT Network Average Outbound Queueing Latency — Average time a message waited in the outbound queue before being sent. Queueing, as opposed to time on the wire.

RDT Network Socket Min Outbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the outbound socket buffer. Low is bad -- this measures headroom remaining, so it reads backwards from every other column. Zero means exhaustion and a stalled transport.

RDT Network Socket Min Inbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the inbound socket buffer. Low is bad, for the same reason.

Keepalive reset (Total) — Lifetime count of keepalive resets: RDT gave up on a peer connection and re-established it. Cumulative since boot, so the number itself means little -- watch whether it is increasing.

Num ready delay (Total) — Lifetime count of delays waiting for a connection to become ready. Cumulative since boot; the trend is the signal.

Transport - per host

Renders the vSAN RDT Transport Per Host view.

RDT Network Max Outbound Context Bytes — The high-water mark of bytes queued for transmit on an RDT context. A rising maximum alongside a healthy average means the transport is bursting into its headroom rather than sitting in it -- the early signal, before queue latency moves. Read it next to txSbSpaceMin: a high maximum with a low buffer minimum is a transport running out of room, and no amount of disk tuning will help.

RDT Network Host Average Latency — Average round-trip latency of vSAN's own transport between hosts. This sits above TCP, so it can be slow while every NIC counter is clean.

RDT Network Host Max Latency — Worst round-trip latency observed. Spikes here matter more than the average -- one stalled transfer blocks whatever was waiting on it.

RDT Network Host Min Latency — Best round-trip latency observed. Useful only as a floor to compare the average against.

RDT Network Average Outbound Queueing Latency — Average time a message waited in the outbound queue before being sent. Queueing, as opposed to time on the wire.

RDT Network Max Outbound Queueing Latency — Worst outbound queueing delay observed.

RDT Network Socket Min Outbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the outbound socket buffer. Low is bad -- this measures headroom remaining, so it reads backwards from every other column. Zero means exhaustion and a stalled transport.

RDT Network Socket Min Inbound Bytes (Low Is Bad) — Lowest free space seen in the inbound socket buffer. Low is bad, for the same reason.

RDT Network Socket Max Inbound Bytes — Highest free space seen inbound. Context for the minimum beside it.

Keepalive reset (Total) — Lifetime count of keepalive resets: RDT gave up on a peer connection and re-established it. Cumulative since boot, so the number itself means little -- watch whether it is increasing.

Num ready delay (Total) — Lifetime count of delays waiting for a connection to become ready. Cumulative since boot; the trend is the signal.
